power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background and aims: In most self-exclusion programs, leaving is the gambler's own decision.
In Chile, by contrast, revocation requires the consent of a sponsor whom the participant nominates at enrollment and may later replace.
We investigated whether the relationship with the first sponsor, and later changes of sponsor, relate to how long participants remain excluded.
Methods: We analyzed records from Chile's self-exclusion registry (2019-2025; N = 3,825 participants; 1,753 revocations).

Time to first revocation was examined using Kaplan-Meier curves and time-varying Cox models including the relationship with the first sponsor, the direction of replacements, and prior rejected requests, accounting for the three-month waiting period after a replacement.

Results: Participants whose first sponsor was a close family member had a lower revocation hazard than those who nominated a partner (HR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.59-0.76); their median time to revocation was 40.4 months, against 20 to 22 months in the other groups.
More importantly, replacing a non-family sponsor with a close family member was followed by a lower hazard (HR = 0.59), whereas the reverse change showed no detectable difference.
Each rejected request, and each replacement once the waiting period had ended, was associated with a higher hazard, with many revocations right after that period.
Discussion and conclusions: Having a close family member as sponsor, whether from enrollment or after a replacement, is associated with longer exclusions.
These results are discussed in the light of the sponsor's role as a social commitment device and the points at which participants may benefit from support.
Consider a person who has been losing money for months in casinos and decides to ban himself from coming back to every casino in the country.
This, which may be beneficial for the individual and their close family, is what voluntary self-exclusion (VSE) programs allow.
In general, after a period of time the ban expires or the person requests to be removed from the list of self-excluded gamblers.
So far, most of the evidence on the decision to self-exclude has come from studies of participants' self-reported motives for enrolling and their gambling behavior prior to enrollment.

In early descriptive work, Ladouceur et al. (2007) and Hayer and Meyer (2010) found that participants frequently cited financial distress, gambling-related problems, and difficulty controlling their gambling as reasons for enrolling.

text.text: Although these observations clarify the circumstances under which people enter self-exclusion, what is less clear is how those circumstances relate to the subsequent duration of the exclusion.
Studies following participants after enrollment suggest that the course of an exclusion can differ from what their initial motives would lead one to expect.

text.text: In this paper we focus on additional circumstances that may influence the decision to revoke an exclusion, and how they relate to the duration of self-exclusion.
One such circumstance concerns the involvement of a sponsor.

In most self-exclusion programs, sponsors or significant others may provide support, receive information, or be contacted when someone attempts to enter a venue (Gainsbury, 2014; Nowatzki and Williams, 2002), but they hold no veto power over the participant's decision to revoke and go back to gambling.

text.text: The Chilean program is a special case, in which the sponsor's consent is required for revocation.

This opens the possibility that the relationship with the sponsor may influence the duration of exclusion, both by influencing the participant's willingness to request revocation and the sponsor's willingness to consent.

In Chile, following the 2005 Gambling Law and the expansion of the casino sector, the Superintendencia de Casinos de Juego (SCJ; Superintendency of Gaming Casinos) was established to regulate casinos and implement harm-minimization policies (Nazer and Llorca-Jaña, 2021).
text.formatted: In Chile, following the 2005 Gambling Law and the expansion of the casino sector, the Superintendencia de Casinos de Juego (SCJ; Superintendency of Gaming Casinos) was established to regulate casinos and implement harm-minimization policies <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Nazer and Llorca-Jaña, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Under its centralized VSE program, launched in August 2019, a gambler who self-excludes cannot enter any licensed casino in the country for an indefinite period.

At enrollment, the participant must nominate a sponsor and declare their relationship to that person, typically a close family member (such as a parent, sibling, or child), a spouse or partner, or a friend.

To leave the program, the participant must wait at least six months from enrollment and submit a revocation request co-signed by the sponsor; if the sponsor does not agree to sign, the exclusion remains in force.

This veto power is the critical feature that distinguishes the Chilean program from most other VSE programs, and it is the feature that we exploit in this paper. 1While an exclusion is in force, the participant can also replace their sponsor at any time (or a sponsor may resign), transferring the power to authorize a revocation to a new person.

text.text: Because a gambler whose current sponsor refuses to sign could use this rule to appoint someone more permissive, the regulation imposes a three-month waiting period after any sponsor replacement during which revocation is not allowed.

If a participant submits a revocation request that does not meet these requirements (for example, before completing the mandatory six-month period, during the three-month waiting period after a replacement, or with an incomplete form), the SCJ rejects the application and the exclusion continues.
Once a revocation is approved, the person is removed from the list of self-excluded gamblers, though they can enroll again in the future if they decide to ban themselves again.
Requiring the sponsor's consent provides a direct mechanism through which the relationship with the sponsor may influence the duration of exclusion.

Research on commitment devices suggests that involving another person can help people maintain a commitment (Bryan et al., 2010) and, as we have already mentioned, pressure from significant others may also play an important role (Motka et al., 2018).

text.text: In the present setting, a parent, sibling, or child may be less willing to authorize a return to casinos than a partner or a friend, or the participant may be more reluctant to ask a close family member for permission to revoke.
Either process should contribute to longer exclusions among participants who nominate close family at enrollment.
This is one of the hypotheses we explore in this paper.
An important difficulty in interpreting differences across initial sponsors, however, is that participants choose whom to nominate when they enroll.

Gamblers who nominate a close family member may differ from those who nominate a partner or a friend in ways that the registry does not record, such as the severity of their gambling problems or how much they want to stop gambling; this is a classic self-selection process.
Those data are not observable.
However, the fact that participants can replace their sponsors during an exclusion allows us to look at the same question in a different way.
Although replacements are also chosen by participants, they occur after the first sponsor has been nominated.

To the extent that the relationship with the sponsor matters, a participant who replaces a partner or a friend with a close family member should become less likely to revoke after that, whereas those that replace a close family member with a partner, a friend or somebody else outside the family should become more likely to revoke.
Likewise, replacing a sponsor or having a request rejected are also markers of intent to leave the program.
Therefore, both of these events should be followed by a higher likelihood of revocation.
These are the other hypotheses we examine in this paper.

To test these predictions, we analyzed the records of Chile's centralized self-exclusion registry, which include all enrollments, sponsor replacements, and revocation requests between August 2019 and June 2025.
We first compared the time to first revocation of participants whose first sponsor was a close family member with that of participants who nominated a partner, a friend, or someone else.
We then used time-varying Cox models to examine whether the likelihood of revocation changed after a participant replaced their sponsor.

We distinguished three types of replacement: those in which a close family member became the sponsor, those in which a close family member was replaced by someone outside the family, and those in which a friend became the sponsor.
These models also took into account how many times each participant had replaced their sponsor and how many of their revocation requests had been rejected.
Because revocation is restricted during the three months that follow a replacement, we examined the likelihood of revocation once those three months had ended.
To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine how the relationship with a sponsor in a context where the sponsor holds veto power over revocation relates to the duration of self-exclusion.
We analyzed records of self-exclusion events from Chile's centralized registry, covering the period from its launch in August 2019 to 12 June 2025.
The SCJ maintains this registry as part of its regulatory responsibilities, recording enrollments, revocations, and changes of sponsor.
Access to the records was obtained under a data-use agreement between ISCI and the SCJ and was facilitated by one co-author (M.S.), who is affiliated with the SCJ.
National identifiers were used only to link records across events and were removed before analysis.
On 12 June 2025, the registry listed 3,401 participants who were currently self-excluded and 1,454 whose exclusions had been revoked.

Many of these participants had entered or left the program more than once: of the 3,401 who were self-excluded, 690 (20.3%) had revoked at least one previous exclusion, and of the 1,454 whose exclusions had been revoked, 305 (21.0%) had already been self-excluded at least once before.
The survival analyses followed each participant from their first accepted enrollment, and the analysis sample was obtained in four steps.

First, after removing duplicate records, we excluded 17 participants whose revocation was signed by a sponsor other than the one on record and 103 participants whose accepted enrollment or revocation had no sponsor recorded; of the remaining participants, 4,734 had an accepted enrollment that was followed for more than one day.

Second, we excluded 903 participants whose first record was loaded on 9 August 2019 from the earlier casinoby-casino system, because their recorded enrollment date reflects the date of that administrative transfer rather than when they originally enrolled, and most of these records lack a valid birth date.
Third, we excluded four participants whose age was missing.

Fourth, we excluded two participants whose revocation was recorded after 50 and 120 days, well before the mandatory six-month period, which we regarded as recording errors; revocations recorded a few days before the six-month mark were kept, since they are likely to reflect differences in how the six months were counted.
The final analysis sample therefore comprised 3,825 participants, of whom 1,753 revoked their first exclusion before 12 June 2025.
Of these participants, 453 enrolled in the six months before 12 June 2025 and therefore could not yet have revoked.

We left them out of the descriptive comparisons between participants who revoked and those who remained excluded (Table 1 and Figure 1), but kept them in the main survival analyses, in which they contribute only the time during which they were observed.

text.text: The primary outcome was the time from a participant's first accepted enrollment to their first accepted revocation, recorded in days and reported in months.
Participants who had not revoked by 12 June 2025 were censored at that date.
Since Circular 102 came into force in August 2019, self-exclusion has been indefinite, with a mandatory minimum period of six months before revocation can be requested.

Our main predictor of interest was the relationship between the participant and the sponsor nominated at first enrollment (the first sponsor), classified as partner (including spouses and domestic partners), close family member (parent, sibling, child, grandparent, or grandchild), friend, or other.

We focused on the first sponsor because this relationship is fixed when follow-up begins, whereas the sponsor in office at a later point in time partly reflects replacements made during the exclusion, which we examined separately.

We also included three demographic characteristics of the participant: sex, age at enrollment, and whether the participant lived in the Metropolitan Region, which includes Santiago (17.6% of the sample).

Although we had no specific predictions for these demographic variables, we included them as controls because they may be related both to the choice of sponsor and to revocation; for example, women nominated a close family member more often than men did, and a partner less often.
Because the administrative registry records participants as male or female, we use the term "sex" throughout.

Four counts of events occurring during the exclusion were entered as time-varying covariates: effective sponsor replacements, in which a different person became the sponsor; fictitious replacements, in which the replacement request named the existing sponsor; sponsor resignations; and rejected revocation requests. 2 Rejected revocations were included as a marker of intent to leave the program: because a request can only be rejected if it was submitted in the first place, this count captures active attempts to revoke, and its hazard ratio should not be interpreted as a causal effect of the rejection itself.

Under Circular 122 (in force since 20 August 2021), a participant may replace their sponsor at any time, and no limit is imposed on the number of replacements.
However, revocation cannot occur within three months of a replacement.
In practice, this three-month waiting period is intended to prevent participants from replacing a sponsor simply to obtain immediate revocation.
Before that date, the regulation did not impose a waiting period after a replacement.
To examine time to first revocation as a function of the relationship with the sponsor, we used survival analysis.
In survival analysis, the variable of interest is the time until an event occurs, in our case the number of days from enrollment to revocation.

This allows us to compute the probability that a participant remains excluded beyond any given time and the hazard, that is, the probability of revoking at a given time among those who are still excluded (Therneau and Grambsch, 2000).

To the extent that a close family member is less willing to consent to revocation, or the participant is less willing to ask a relative for it, participants whose first sponsor was a close family member should be less likely to revoke than those who nominated a partner; that is, β 1 < 0 (a hazard ratio below 1).

Note that counting a replacement from the day it was recorded would combine the three-month period during which revocation is restricted with the unrestricted period that follows.

We therefore entered each replacement made on or after 20 August 2021, effective or fictitious, into E i (t) or F i (t) three months after it was recorded, while W i (t) captured the three-month waiting period itself.
Replacements made before that date, when there was no waiting period, were entered from the day they were recorded.
For example, if a participant replaced their sponsor on day 300 of the exclusion, W i (t) took the value 1 from day 300 to day 390, and the replacement was added to E i (t) from day 391 onwards.
In this way, the replacement coefficients describe the hazard once the waiting period has ended.

To test whether changes of sponsor during an exclusion had a similar effect, we extended Equation 1 by adding one or more of three time-varying indicators for the direction of effective replacements: Towards i (t), equal to 1 once the participant had replaced someone outside the family with a close family member (towards family); Away i (t), equal to 1 once the participant had replaced a close family member with someone outside the family (away from family); and FriendEntry i (t), equal to 1 once the participant had replaced a sponsor who was not a friend with a friend (friend entry).
In all three definitions, partners were classified as outside the close family.

Each indicator took the value 0 before the first replacement of that kind and 1 from then on, starting when the three-month waiting period ended (or on the day of the replacement, for replacements made before 20 August 2021), and remained 1 if the participant later changed sponsor again.
Under the hypothesis that the relationship with the sponsor matters, the coefficient on Towards i (t) should be negative and that on Away i (t) should be positive.
Because these models also include E i (t), each directional indicator compares replacements in one direction with replacements in other directions, rather than with making no replacement.
Importantly, these labels describe only the change in relationship category; the sponsor's willingness to consent was not measured.

Across all five models, having a close family member as the first sponsor, effective replacements, and prior rejected requests remained strongly associated with revocation.

The present study shows that, when leaving a self-exclusion program requires the consent of a sponsor, the relationship with that person is closely related to the duration of the exclusion.
This was the case both for the sponsor nominated at enrollment and for the sponsor brought in during the course of the exclusion.

Participants whose first sponsor was a close family member had a lower revocation hazard than those who nominated a partner, and half of them were still excluded more than three years after enrolling, nearly twice as long as participants in the other groups.

More importantly, changes of sponsor during the exclusion pointed in the same direction: participants who replaced a sponsor outside the family with a close family member had a lower hazard after the change than those who made other replacements, whereas replacing a relative with someone outside the family was not reliably followed by a higher hazard.
By contrast, replacements in general were followed by a higher hazard once the three-month waiting period had ended, and revocations were concentrated in the days immediately after that period.

Previous reviews of self-exclusion programs have documented reductions in gambling behavior and problem severity, along with improvements in psychological wellbeing (Gainsbury, 2014; Kotter et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Previous reviews of self-exclusion programs have documented reductions in gambling behavior and problem severity, along with improvements in psychological wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Gainsbury, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kotter et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In spite of these benefits, outcomes vary considerably across studies, and some participants try to enter casinos while they are excluded or continue gambling.
Because much of this evidence comes from observational studies without control groups, it is often difficult to separate the contribution of self-exclusion from other changes in participants' lives.

For example, McCormick et al. (2018) observed reductions in gambling symptoms during exclusion, but noted that these improvements were smaller among participants who tried to enter casinos while they were excluded.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">McCormick et al. (2018)</ref> observed reductions in gambling symptoms during exclusion, but noted that these improvements were smaller among participants who tried to enter casinos while they were excluded.

text.text: In this regard, an outstanding question is what leads participants to maintain, or end, an exclusion once they have enrolled.

When Pickering and Blaszczynski (2022) compared people who renewed their self-exclusion with those who discontinued it, they found no detectable differences across the demographic, gambling, and psychological measures they examined, and called for further research on social and environmental influences on this decision.
Here, we examined one such influence: the relationship with the person whose consent is required to revoke.

Chile's registry makes this analysis possible by recording initial sponsor relationships, subsequent replacements, and revocation histories within a program where exclusion does not expire automatically.

In the broader literature on gambling treatment and recovery, Petry and Weiss (2009) and Penfold and Ogden (2024) have shown that social support is associated with lower gambling severity and better quality of life.
text.formatted: In the broader literature on gambling treatment and recovery, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Petry and Weiss (2009)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Penfold and Ogden (2024)</ref> have shown that social support is associated with lower gambling severity and better quality of life.

text.text: The present findings concern a more specific arrangement, in which another person holds formal veto power over the decision to revoke.
Under this view, a parent, sibling, or child may be less willing to authorize revocation, or the participant may be more reluctant to request it from that relative.
Either possibility is consistent with the idea that involving another person can help people maintain a commitment (Bryan et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Either possibility is consistent with the idea that involving another person can help people maintain a commitment <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bryan et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: An alternative explanation, however, can be drawn from the fact that participants choose their own sponsors.

Those who nominate a relative at enrollment may have less severe gambling problems, may be more motivated to stop gambling, or may have different family circumstances than those who nominate a partner, and these baseline differences could produce longer exclusions without any active role for the sponsor.
Although our observational records cannot rule out self-selection of this kind, the analysis of sponsor replacements makes a simple baseline account harder to accept.
Replacements occur after the first sponsor has been chosen, and our models compared replacements in different directions while adjusting for the relationship with the first sponsor.

Even so, participants who brought in a close family member had a lower hazard after the replacement than those who made other replacements, and this difference disappeared when the sponsor in office at each point in time was used instead of the first sponsor; in that model, having a close family member in office was itself associated with a lower hazard.
In other words, the lower hazard was related to having a close family member as sponsor, whether from enrollment or after a replacement.

Participants also choose whom to bring in, of course, but unmeasured differences between participants would then have to produce the same relationship pattern at two different points of the exclusion.
What is less clear is why the two directions of replacement differed.
Replacing a relative with someone outside the family was not reliably followed by a higher hazard, whereas bringing in a friend was.

One possibility is that choosing a close family member as the first sponsor reflects how much the participant wants to stop gambling, and that this does not change when the relative is later replaced.
Because our models include the relationship with the first sponsor, this effect remains after the replacement, and replacing the relative adds little to the hazard.
By contrast, those who bring in a friend may more often do so in order to obtain consent to revoke.
Because the registry does not record the reasons for replacements, these ideas can only be regarded as informal speculations.
Prior rejected requests were also strongly associated with revocation.

Naturally, this result should not be taken to mean that a rejection causes revocation: a rejected request can only occur once a participant has applied to revoke, and it therefore indicates that the participant has already decided to leave the program.
In many cases, the participant simply applies again after correcting an administrative error or waiting until the time requirements are met.
The same applies to sponsor replacements.

Once the three-month waiting period had ended, the hazard after an effective replacement was more than three times higher, and a large number of revocations took place in the days immediately after that period expired.

Before Circular 122 came into force in August 2021, by contrast, revocation could follow a replacement without delay, and most participants who revoked after a replacement made in that period did so within three months of it.

While it is not unreasonable to think that many participants replace their sponsor in order to revoke, some replacements are likely to follow changes in the participant's life that the registry does not record, such as the death of a relative or the end of a relationship.
Moreover, many participants entered and left the program more than once: on 12 June 2025, one in five of those who were self-excluded had revoked a previous exclusion.
In practical terms, these findings suggest several ways in which programs that involve a sponsor might be strengthened.
Because how long an exclusion lasts depends on the sponsor's consent, sponsors should receive clear guidance at enrollment about their role and the conditions under which revocation can be requested.
Ideally, this should be subject to continuous follow-up to ensure the sponsors are updated about their role.

Working directly with sponsors, including those of participants who remain excluded and of those who revoked, as well as sponsors who were replaced and those who replaced them, would also be valuable.
Not only would this help to strengthen the sponsor-gambler commitment, but also help regulatory and research institutions understand the underlying causes of each type of event.
In addition, events recorded during the exclusion can serve as early signals that a participant is preparing to leave the program.
Because a rejected request marks an active intent to revoke, it identifies participants who may benefit from both clarification of the application procedure and additional support.

Similarly, the large number of revocations at the end of the three-month waiting period indicates that this restriction delays, rather than prevents, many of the revocations that follow a replacement; the replacement request itself may therefore serve as an opportunity to offer support.

These considerations are in line with recommendations to provide support alongside self-exclusion (Gainsbury, 2014) and with reports from Pickering and Blaszczynski (2022) that participants often feel insufficiently supported when deciding whether to renew or discontinue their agreements.

text.text: Several limitations should be noted.

Because participants choose both their initial sponsors and any subsequent replacements, the differences we observe across relationship categories may partly reflect unmeasured differences in gambling severity, motivation to stop gambling, or family circumstances, as well as the underlying reasons for changing sponsors rather than the new sponsor's response to a request.

Furthermore, because rejected requests reflect an active intent to leave the program, adjusting for them may take away part of the association of other variables, such as the relationship with the sponsor, that act by making participants less likely to request revocation in the first place.

The proportional-hazards assumption also did not hold for some covariates, including the relationship with the first sponsor, meaning that the corresponding hazard ratios should be interpreted as average differences over the follow-up period.
Finally, ending an exclusion need not imply a return to harmful gambling, just as remaining on the register need not imply abstinence (Slutske et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Finally, ending an exclusion need not imply a return to harmful gambling, just as remaining on the register need not imply abstinence <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Slutske et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: As shown by Turner et al. (2021) in their study of gamblers reinstating after an exclusion, directly assessing post-exclusion gambling behavior is essential for evaluating harm-minimization outcomes.

text.text: Because our survival analyses were restricted to the first revocation and relied solely on administrative records, following participants across successive exclusions and linking registry events to clinical or behavioral measures of gambling would help clarify how sponsor barriers relate to long-term recovery.
To summarize, in this paper we have tested the idea that the relationship with a sponsor may influence the duration of gambling self-exclusion.

Our findings show that when leaving selfexclusion requires the consent of another person, nominating or switching to a close family member is associated with remaining excluded for substantially longer, whereas sponsor replacements and rejected requests mark moments at which participants are likely to leave the program.

Chile's registry allows these social barriers to be tracked over time, and suggests that the relationship with the sponsor is a variable that is important to consider in the design of self-exclusion programs.
